blocks.text: Luminosity is the total amount of energy emitted by a star per unit time in the form of electromagnetic radiations. It is a fundamental property that defines the intrinsic brightness of a star. Luminosity is represented by the symbol L and is measured in watts, indicating the total power of radiation emitted by a star. Luminosity of a star primarily depends on its radius and surface temperature. Larger stars have more surface area to emit radiations and therefore, tend to be more luminous. Similarly, for stars of equal size, the one with the higher surface temperature will radiate more energy and hence, exhibits greater luminosity. The luminosity of a star can be represented as the product of its surface area (A=4πr²) and radiant intensity (I = σT⁴);

blocks.title: Tidbit!
blocks.text: The Sun shines with an immense luminosity of about 4×10²⁶ watts that is equivalent to billions of nuclear explosions happening every second.
Equation (21.1) is called Stefan-Boltzmann law. It states that;

blocks.title: Stefan-Boltzmann law
blocks.text: The total output power of a star is proportional to the product of its surface area and the fourth power of its temperature.

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: Stefan-Boltzmann's law helps astronomers estimate the size and brightness of stars just by knowing their temperature.
where σ is Stefan-Boltzmann constant. Its value is 5.67×10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴. T is the surface temperature and r is the radius of the star.

blocks.title: Example 21.1
blocks.problem: The luminosity of a star is given as 2.5 × 10²⁶ W, and its surface temperature is 6000 K. Estimate the radius of the star.
steps: Luminosity of the star L = 2.5 × 10²⁶ W
Surface temperature of the star T = 6000 K
Using Stefan-Boltzmann law; L = 4πr² σ T⁴
